land.text: Upper Peru, 'the newly independent Alto Peru'

predecessors.note: Cliopatria's Spanish Empire row ends here for Upper Peru; the Rio de la Plata dossier also lists Bolivia among its successors (Upper Peru was in that viceroyalty from 1776, per the History of Bolivia page).

land.text: Upper Peru, which the United Provinces never retook

predecessors.note: Named as a predecessor because the Rio de la Plata dossier hands Upper Peru to Bolivia; the territory was Spanish-held in 1825.

capitals.name: Sucre (La Plata, Chuquisaca)
capitals.note: Proclaimed 'the provisional capital of the newly independent Alto Peru' on 1 July 1826 (renamed for Sucre); a law of 12 July 1839 named Sucre the capital. Still the constitutional capital.

capitals.name: La Paz
capitals.note: Seat of government from 1898: the La Paz page says 'In 1898, La Paz was made the de facto seat of the national government', 'with Sucre remaining the nominal historical as well as judiciary capital'. The Bolivia page says only that the seat 'moved to La Paz at the start of the twentieth century' (no year); the dated page is used.

keyframe_review.note: 1.81 M km2 for 1825-1835. The page gives no area at independence but says 'Since independence, Bolivia has lost over half of its territory to neighboring countries'; against the infobox's 1,098,581 km2 that implies more than 2.2 M km2, so the shape (1.65 times today's area) is within a factor of two and stands as a lower bound. By the gazetteer it holds the Litoral on the Pacific (Antofagasta, 306 cells), Acre, 635 cells of Brazil's Amazonas, parts of Mato Grosso and the whole Paraguayan Chaco (Boquerón, Alto Paraguay, Presidente Hayes): the Chaco is a claim, since 'The Gran Chaco had been a disputed territory since 1810' (Gran Chaco page, opened for the Argentine dossier). 'Declared: 6 August 1825' (infobox). Tarija is inside: the Confederation page says Bolivia 'occupied and annexed' it before Argentina declared war on 19 May 1837 but gives no year, while the Tarija Department page says 'Between 1816 and 1898, the region was part of Argentina, and was ceded to Bolivia in exchange for Puna de Atacama' (Argentine title surrendered in 1898, see the ledger's Puna event; the pages conflict on 1825, and the year of annexation is not on any page opened, so the shape's 1825 start stands). Unverified: page budget (no page gives the 1825 boundary). Presidente Hayes (the Chaco bank opposite Asuncion; 312-313 of this shape's cells, about 79,000 km2) was not held by Bolivia in fact: the Villa Hayes page has Villa Occidental founded under Carlos Antonio Lopez's government (1841-1862) after the French colony of Nueva Burdeos, and 'Argentine soldiers occupied the city during the Paraguayan War' (late 1860s; the page gives no 1869-1879 span); the Presidente Hayes Department page has Hayes 'ultimately awarded the territory to Paraguay in 1878'. The cell block is a Bolivian claim here (soft); from 1878 it is removed (keyframes 5-10) because the Paraguay dossier draws it Paraguayan.

Identical to the 1825 outline (1.81 M km2) for 1840-1864. Cliopatria covers 1836-1839 with the Peru-Bolivian Confederation row, in which Bolivia was one of three states ('a loose confederation made up of three states: North Peru, South Peru, and the Bolivian Republic'); the ledger records the 28 October 1836 decree and the 1839 dissolution, and this shape resumes in 1840 (Velasco declared the Confederation dissolved on 26 October 1839). No page opened dates a border change between 1840 and 1864. Presidente Hayes (about 79,000 km2 of this shape) is a Bolivian claim only: Villa Occidental, founded under Carlos Antonio Lopez (1841-1862), was a Paraguayan town on that bank and Argentine soldiers occupied it in the late 1860s (Villa Hayes page); it is removed from 1878 (keyframes 5-10).

1,815,658 km2 for 1865 alone, 3,363 km2 (0.2 percent) above the neighbouring years, with the eastern bbox edge shifted by 0.007 degrees: a one-year artifact. No page opened dates a Bolivian border change in 1865 or 1866 (no page opened places Bolivia in any 1865 event). Presidente Hayes (about 79,000 km2 of this shape) is a Bolivian claim only: Villa Occidental, founded under Carlos Antonio Lopez (1841-1862), was a Paraguayan town on that bank and Argentine soldiers occupied it in the late 1860s (Villa Hayes page); it is removed from 1878 (keyframes 5-10).

The old outline (1.81 M km2) to 26 March 1867. Cliopatria keeps it through 1867 although the Treaty of Ayacucho is dated 27 March 1867 (infobox 'Signed: 27 March 1867'); the next shape therefore starts in 1867 (ledger: loss to Brazil, March 1867). Presidente Hayes (about 79,000 km2 of this shape) is a Bolivian claim only: Villa Occidental, founded under Carlos Antonio Lopez (1841-1862), was a Paraguayan town on that bank and Argentine soldiers occupied it in the late 1860s (Villa Hayes page); it is removed from 1878 (keyframes 5-10). The 1866 treaty with Chile set the boundary 'at the 24th parallel' with a shared-revenue zone between 23 and 25 degrees S, and the 1874 treaty (6 August 1874) kept the parallel (Boundary Treaty of 1874 page); the shape's Litoral stops at 23.92 S, so it already agrees with that line and no cell changes.

correction.text: shape unchanged; it holds from 27 March 1867 (Treaty of Ayacucho), not from 1868. Acre stays Bolivian until 1903

keyframe_review.note: 1.575 M km2: the outline after the treaty with Brazil, 237,233 km2 below the old one. By the gazetteer the loss is 616 of the 635 Amazonas cells and the Mato Grosso and Rondonia slices, with Acre kept (541 of 551 cells), which agrees with the pages: the treaty 'assigned the land of Acre ... to Bolivia in exchange for 102,400 square kilometers' (Treaty of Ayacucho) and 'had yielded 164,242 square kilometers' annexed to Amazonas (Acre War). The three figures disagree (102,400, 164,242, 237,233); the shape's own figure is the largest, and the pages give no boundary line. Only the start year changes: the shape holds from March 1867, not 1868. Presidente Hayes (about 79,000 km2 of this shape) is a Bolivian claim only: Villa Occidental, founded under Carlos Antonio Lopez (1841-1862), was a Paraguayan town on that bank and Argentine soldiers occupied it in the late 1860s (Villa Hayes page); it is removed from 1878 (keyframes 5-10).

1,575,470 km2 for 1877-1879, 408 km2 above the 1868 shape (a trivial redraw). The Litoral (Antofagasta) is inside and still Bolivian until the Chilean landing of 14 February 1879 (ledger); the 1874 treaty of 6 August 1874 had kept the 24th parallel (Boundary Treaty of 1874 page). Corrected: 313 of the shape's gazetteer cells (about 79,000 km2) are Paraguay's Presidente Hayes department, which the Paraguay dossier draws as Paraguayan from the 1878 award (its /ledger/16 and paraguay_1877 correction); the Presidente Hayes Department page says Hayes 'ultimately awarded the territory to Paraguay in 1878', so Bolivia is drawn without it from 1878 and the double drawing goes. Source: Presidente Hayes Department page; Villa Hayes page for the Paraguayan town of Villa Occidental on that bank.

minus.text: the Chaco awarded to Paraguay by President Hayes in 1878; the department is named for him

correction.text: Bolivia's 1877 shape without the Presidente Hayes department, which Hayes awarded to Paraguay in 1878; the correction holds from 1878 (1877 stays as drawn). The Litoral is still Bolivian until 14 February 1879

minus.text: Paraguayan from the Hayes award of 1878

correction.text: shape without Presidente Hayes (Paraguayan from 1878), with the Litoral (Antofagasta region) under Chilean occupation from 14 February 1879: hatched, not Bolivian-controlled

keyframe_review.note: 1,575,216 km2. The shape still holds the Litoral, where Chile 'occupied without resistance the Bolivian port city of Antofagasta' on 14 February 1879; Bolivia and Chile were at war from 1 March 1879 and 'Bolivia withdrew after the Battle of Tacna, on 26 May 1880'. The land stays Bolivian in law but under Chilean occupation: the ledger carries the occupation, so the Litoral is to be drawn hatched. Presidente Hayes (313 cells, about 79,000 km2) is removed as in the 1877 keyframe: Paraguay's from the 1878 award.

minus.text: Paraguayan from the Hayes award of 1878

correction.text: shape without Presidente Hayes (Paraguayan from 1878), with the Litoral under Chilean occupation (truce of 4 April 1884) until the treaty of October 1904, and Acre in the shape until 17 November 1903

keyframe_review.note: 1,575,300 km2 for 1885-1904. 'On 4 April 1884, a truce was signed with Chile' and the War of the Pacific page has Bolivia accepting 'the military occupation of the entire Bolivian coast'; the shape therefore keeps the Litoral for 20 years of occupation that ended only with the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of October 1904. Acre is inside and goes in 1903. Presidente Hayes is removed as in the 1877 keyframe. The rest of the Chaco Boreal (Boquerón and Alto Paraguay) stays as a soft Bolivian claim: the Chaco War page has Bolivia found Puerto Pacheco in 1885 and the Paraguayan gunboat Pirapo 'forcibly evicted the Bolivians from the settlement' in 1888, so no Bolivian hold on the river is dated after 1888.

1,329,255 km2 for 1905-1925: Acre (191,000 km2 per the Treaty of Petropolis page, signed 17 November 1903) and the Litoral (Treaty of Peace and Friendship, October 1904) are both out (6 of 551 Acre cells, 10 of 487 Antofagasta cells remain). Against the infobox 1,098,581 km2 the ratio is 1.21; the gap is the Chaco (1,030 cells of the shape in Paraguay: 313 in Presidente Hayes, which is Paraguayan from 1878 and is now removed, and 717 in Boquerón and Alto Paraguay, the Chaco Boreal that Paraguay won by 1935). Without Presidente Hayes the shape is about 79,000 km2 smaller (about 1.25 M km2, ratio about 1.14 to the infobox). The Bolivia page says 'Through diplomatic channels in 1909, it lost the basin of the Madre de Dios River, yielding 250,000 km2 to Peru'; the shape never held that basin (8 of Madre de Dios's 292 cells) and shows no change in 1909. The Chaco War page puts Bolivian outposts on the Pilcomayo from 1905 ('founded Ballivian and Guachalla, two new outposts along the Pilcomayo River in the Chaco') while 'both Paraguayan and Argentine ranchers were already breeding cattle and exploiting the quebracho forests in the area' and the Mennonite colonies settled under Paraguayan rule in the 1920s: the Boquerón and Alto Paraguay block is a claim, not a hold.

minus.text: Paraguayan from the Hayes award of 1878

correction.text: shape without Presidente Hayes (Paraguayan since 1878); Boquerón and Alto Paraguay stay as the Bolivian Chaco Boreal claim to 1935

keyframe_review.note: 1,329,119 km2 for 1926-1928, 136 km2 below the 1905 shape, the western bbox edge moving 0.05 degrees east: a boundary adjustment on the Peruvian side that no page opened dates (the Bolivia-Peru relations page has nothing on borders). Presidente Hayes (313 cells, about 79,000 km2) is removed as in the 1877 keyframe.

minus.text: Paraguayan from the Hayes award of 1878

correction.text: shape without Presidente Hayes (Paraguayan since 1878); Boquerón and Alto Paraguay stay as the Bolivian Chaco Boreal claim to 1935

keyframe_review.note: 1,329,147 km2 for 1929-1935, 28 km2 above the 1926 shape: a trivial redraw on the Peruvian side; no page opened dates it. Still holds the Chaco Boreal until the ceasefire of 12 June 1935. Presidente Hayes (313 cells, about 79,000 km2) is removed as in the 1877 keyframe.

minus.text: Paraguayan from the Hayes award of 1878

correction.text: shape without Presidente Hayes (Paraguayan since 1878); Boquerón and Alto Paraguay stay as the Bolivian Chaco Boreal claim to 1935

keyframe_review.note: 1,085,071 km2 for 1936-1952, 0.99 of the infobox's 1,098,581 km2. The drop of 244,076 km2 from 1935 is the Chaco Boreal plus Presidente Hayes (about 79,000 km2 of it, Paraguayan since 1878 and no longer drawn Bolivian after the 1877-1929 corrections, so the drop that is a Bolivian loss in 1935 is about 165,000 km2, Boquerón and Alto Paraguay): the war ended with a ceasefire on 12 June 1935 and the Chaco Peace Conference of July 1938 awarded 'three-fourths of the Gran Chaco' to Paraguay while Bolivia kept the land 'which bordered Puerto Busch'. The shape drops the Chaco in 1936 although the treaty is of 1938; the ledger dates the de facto loss to 1935.

Identical to 1936 (1,085,071 km2) for 1953-2023; the infobox gives 1,098,581 km2 (ratio 0.99). No page opened dates a border change after 1938; the final Chaco demarcation was signed on 28 April 2009 (Chaco War page).

region.text: Upper Peru ('Alto Peru') as the newly independent Bolivian republic

ledger.note: 1825: a congress in Upper Peru declares Bolivia independent. Infobox 'Declared: 6 August 1825'; the republic was named 'in honor of Simón Bolívar'. The page gives no boundary; the region is Cliopatria's 1825 shape.

region.text: the Bolivian Republic, one of the three states of the Confederation

ledger.note: 28 October 1836: Santa Cruz decrees the Peru-Bolivian Confederation at Lima. 'Santa Cruz decreed the establishment of the Peru-Bolivian Confederation, by decree given in Lima on 28 October 1836'; the Confederation was 'made up of three states: North Peru, South Peru, and the Bolivian Republic', so Bolivia is drawn inside the Confederation's shape (Cliopatria row 1836-1839).

region.text: Bolivia after the Confederation, with Tarija, which the page says remained in Bolivia

ledger.note: 26 October 1839: Bolivia leaves the dissolved Confederation. The page says Santa Cruz 'was defeated in the Battle of Yungay on 20 January 1839', Gamarra announced the dissolution on 25 August and a footnote has Velasco declaring the Confederation dissolved on 26 October 1839. The year and the Bolivian date are the page's; Cliopatria's Bolivia row resumes in 1840 and the Peru dossier dates the restoration to January 1839.

region.text: southern Peru: Tacna, Arica, Tarapaca, Moquegua and Puno

ledger.note: 1841: after Ingavi the Bolivian army invades southern Peru. Gamarra's invasion of Bolivia was beaten at Ingavi on 18 November 1841 and the Bolivian army then 'invaded southern Peru'; the page gives no date for the entry, so the year is the page's and the span of land (Tacna, Arica, Tarapaca, then Moquegua and Puno) is my reading.

region.text: southern Peru: Tacna, Arica, Tarapaca, Moquegua and Puno

ledger.note: 7 June 1842: the Treaty of Puno ends the war and the occupation. 'The Treaty of Puno was signed on 7 June 1842, ending the war' (Bolivia page); the Battle of Ingavi page has 'Bolivian troops vacated Tacna, Arica and Tarapaca in February 1842 and retreated to Moquegua and Puno' and does not date the last withdrawal, so the end is bridged to the treaty.

region.text: the Amazonas, Mato Grosso and Rondonia land ceded to the Empire of Brazil by the 1867 treaty (Cliopatria's 1866 shape minus its 1868 shape)

ledger.note: 27 March 1867: the Treaty of Ayacucho with Brazil. Infobox 'Signed: 27 March 1867'; it 'assigned the land of Acre ... to Bolivia in exchange for 102,400 square kilometers of territory'; the Acre War page says it 'had yielded 164,242 square kilometers' annexed to Amazonas. The region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1866 and 1868 shapes (Amazonas, Mato Grosso and Rondonia slices); the pages name no boundary.

region.text: the Bolivian Litoral: the Antofagasta region without Chile's own 1879 land

ledger.note: 14 February 1879: Chile seizes Antofagasta. Chilean troops 'occupied without resistance the Bolivian port city of Antofagasta' on the day of the planned auction of the confiscated company's assets; Bolivia and Chile were at war from 1 March 1879 and Chile occupied the Litoral for 25 years. Bolivia kept the sovereignty in law: the truce of 4 April 1884 (Bolivia page) left Chile administering the coast.

region.text: the Puna de Atacama, Bolivian land occupied by Chile during the Pacific war, exchanged with Argentina

ledger.note: 1898: Bolivia gives up its title to the Puna de Atacama to Argentina. The Tarija Department page says 'Between 1816 and 1898, the region was part of Argentina, and was ceded to Bolivia in exchange for Puna de Atacama' (the exchange year is that page's 1898; the page does not date the Puna transfer itself, hence confidence 2). The Boundary treaty of 1881 page says the Puna lawsuit of 1899 'originated from transfers between Bolivia and Argentina of land occupied by Chile during the Pacific war', so Bolivia held no Puna land on the ground after the Chilean occupation of 1879 and this is a cession of title, not of held land; the 1899 award itself was between Argentina and Chile and belongs to argentine-confederation and republic-of-chile. The Bolivia shape holds only a few Puna cells, so the map effect is small.

1898: the seat of government moves from Sucre to La Paz. The La Paz page: 'In 1898, La Paz was made the de facto seat of the national government', with Sucre remaining the nominal historical and judiciary capital; the Bolivia page says only that it 'moved to La Paz at the start of the twentieth century' (no year), which the dated page supersedes.

region.text: the Acre territory

ledger.note: 14 July 1899: the Republic of Acre is proclaimed against Bolivian rule. Luis Galvez 'proclaimed the Republic of Acre on July 14, 1899', after a revolt led by Jose de Carvalho on 30 April 1899; 'Brazil and Peru also claimed the territory and strongly disapproved of the lease act' of 11 June 1901. The counterpart is the rebel state (no Cliopatria row; a dossier is needed). The contest runs to 15 March 1900, restarts in November 1900 and again on 6 August 1902 (the next events); between those dates Bolivia held Acre without a rebel government.

region.text: the Acre territory

ledger.note: 15 March 1900: the first Republic of Acre ends. 'On March 15, 1900, a Brazilian war flotilla reached Puerto Alonso, arrested Galvez, and dissolved the Republic of Acre'; Bolivia holds Acre without a rebel government until the next rising.

region.text: the Acre territory

ledger.note: November 1900: a second rising against Bolivia. 'In November 1900, another rebellion took place to take Acre from Bolivia', a force 'under the command of journalist Orlando Correa Lopes'; the page gives no day and the force held no state of its own, so the start is bridged to the month of the rising.

region.text: the Acre territory

ledger.note: December 1900: Bolivia defeats the second rising. 'Around Christmas 1900, this force attacked Puerto Alonso' and the Bolivian military beat it; a Bolivian vessel reinforced the Puerto Alonso garrison on 29 December 1900. The page gives no exact day, so December is the page's 'around Christmas'.

region.text: the Acre territory

ledger.note: 6 August 1902: Placido de Castro's campaign begins. 'At 5 a.m. on August 6, 1902, Castro led 33 riflemen in canoes on the Acre River'; Bolivia had leased the region to the Bolivian Trading Company on 11 June 1901.

region.text: the Acre territory

ledger.note: 17 November 1903: the Acre fighting ends with the Treaty of Petropolis. The Acre War page has a preliminary treaty of 21 March 1903, the Third Republic of Acre proclaimed on 27 January 1903 and 'Petropolis on November 17, 1903'. This closes the contest that restarted on 6 August 1902 (the Third Republic of Acre was proclaimed on 27 January 1903).

region.text: the territory of Acre, 191,000 km2

ledger.note: 17 November 1903: Bolivia cedes Acre to Brazil. 'The Treaty of Petropolis, signed on November 17, 1903' 'gave Brazil the territory of Acre (191,000 km2)' (the Acre War page puts it at about 191,000 km2 and dates a ratification to 11 November 1903, which conflicts).

region.text: over 3,000 km2 of Brazilian territory between the Abuna River and Madeira River

ledger.note: 17 November 1903: Bolivia receives a strip from Brazil in the same treaty: 'in exchange for over 3,000 km2 of Brazilian territory between the Abuna River and Madeira River', GBP 2 million and a pledged railway from Riberalta to Porto Velho.

region.text: the Bolivian Litoral, Antofagasta region

ledger.note: October 1904: Bolivia cedes the Litoral to Chile. The 1904 Treaty of Peace and Friendship 'established definite boundaries' and ceded the complete Antofagasta region to Chile (the War of the Pacific page gives only the year; the month is from the Bolivia page: 'In October 1904, the Treaty of Peace and Friendship was signed').

region.text: the Bolivian Litoral, Antofagasta region

ledger.note: October 1904: the Chilean occupation of the Litoral ends in annexation.

region.text: the basin of the Madre de Dios River

ledger.note: 1909: the Madre de Dios basin goes to Peru. 'Through diplomatic channels in 1909, it lost the basin of the Madre de Dios River, yielding 250,000 km2 to Peru.' The Cliopatria shape never held this basin, so the loss changes no cell.

region.text: the Chaco Boreal north of the Hayes award: Boqueron and Alto Paraguay, as in the Paraguay dossier

ledger.note: 15 June 1932: the Chaco fighting begins. A Bolivian detachment captured and burned Fortin Carlos Antonio Lopez at Pitiantuta Lake (the page does not treat this as the start date: the infobox gives 9 September 1932); the page's infobox and the first major battle (Boqueron, 9 September 1932) start later, and the Paraguay dossier dates the contest to this incident. The zone is Boqueron plus Alto Paraguay only: Presidente Hayes was Paraguayan from the 1878 award (Presidente Hayes Department page), so it is not part of the Chaco War zone.

region.text: the Chaco Boreal north of the Hayes award: Boqueron and Alto Paraguay, as in the Paraguay dossier

ledger.note: 12 June 1935: the ceasefire ends the Chaco War. 'On 12 June, the day that the ceasefire agreement was signed, Paraguayan troops were entrenched only 15 km away from the Bolivian oil fields.' The zone is Boqueron plus Alto Paraguay only: Presidente Hayes was Paraguayan from the 1878 award (Presidente Hayes Department page), so it is not part of the Chaco War zone.

region.text: the Chaco Boreal, three-fourths of the Gran Chaco: Boqueron and Alto Paraguay without the land Bolivia kept (Puerto Busch)

ledger.note: 1935: Paraguay holds the Chaco Boreal. The page has the Paraguayan assault on Villa Montes failing in February 1935 and the troops still entrenched 15 km from the Bolivian oil fields at the ceasefire; the Chaco Peace Conference of Buenos Aires in July 1938 awarded 'three-fourths of the Gran Chaco' to Paraguay while Bolivia kept the remainder 'which bordered Puerto Busch' and river rights. The de facto loss is dated to the ceasefire, the treaty to 1938; the page's '52,000 km2' is garbled (Cliopatria's drop is 244,076 km2). After review the region is Boqueron plus Alto Paraguay (719 gazetteer cells) minus the land Bolivia's 1936 shape keeps, mirroring paraguay /ledger/17-19; Presidente Hayes (313 cells) is no longer part of it because the Paraguay dossier draws it Paraguayan from 1878. The 1935-1936 drop also holds about 35 other cells at the edge of the Chaco (27 in Argentina, 2 in Paraguay outside these departments, 4 in Bolivia), a boundary redraw that is not a loss event.

wars.name: Peru-Bolivian Confederation war
wars.outcome: The Restoration Army under Bulnes and Gamarra beat Santa Cruz at Yungay on 20 January 1839; the Confederation was dissolved in 1839 and Bolivia resumed its own course (Velasco, 26 October 1839). Argentina declared war on 19 May 1837 (the Bolivia page says 9 May); Chile on 26 December 1836 (the Bolivia page says 28 December). Tarija remained in Bolivia.
wars.note: No border moved except the Confederation's own creation and end, so the zones are empty; the Treaty of Puno (7 June 1842) ended a later Bolivian-Peruvian war (Bolivia page), not opened.

wars.name: War of 1841 between Peru and Bolivia

zones.text: southern Peru occupied by the Bolivian army after Ingavi

wars.outcome: Gamarra's invasion of Bolivia was defeated at Ingavi on 18 November 1841 (Gamarra killed); the Bolivian army invaded southern Peru, vacated Tacna, Arica and Tarapaca in February 1842 and retreated to Moquegua and Puno; the Treaty of Puno of 7 June 1842 ended the war.
wars.note: The Ingavi page does not mention the Treaty of Puno; its date is from the Bolivia page. No border changed hands: the Bolivian occupation is the ledger's occupation pair. republic-of-peru has no matching event.

wars.name: War of the Pacific
wars.outcome: Chile won: it seized Antofagasta on 14 February 1879, Bolivia withdrew after Tacna (26 May 1880), the 1884 truce left Chile administering the coast and the 1904 treaty ceded the Antofagasta region.
wars.note: Peru's losses (Tarapaca, Tacna and Arica) are in the Peru and Chile dossiers.

wars.name: Acre War
wars.outcome: Brazil won: the Treaty of Petropolis (17 November 1903) gave it Acre for over 3,000 km2 between the Abuna and Madeira rivers, GBP 2 million and a railway.
wars.note: Phases: the first Republic of Acre (14 July 1899 to 15 March 1900), the second rising (November to about Christmas 1900), then Placido de Castro's campaign from 6 August 1902 (Third Republic 27 January 1903) to Petropolis; between them Bolivia held Acre without a rebel government (the ledger's contest events follow these phases). Bolivia leased the region to a trading company on 11 June 1901 and Brazil and Peru also claimed it.

wars.name: Chaco War

zones.text: the Chaco Boreal: Boqueron and Alto Paraguay (Presidente Hayes was Paraguayan from 1878)

wars.outcome: Paraguayan victory: the ceasefire of 12 June 1935 and the Buenos Aires settlement of July 1938 gave Paraguay three-fourths of the Chaco Boreal; Bolivia kept the land bordering Puerto Busch and river rights.
wars.note: Fighting began with the incident of 15 June 1932; the first major battle was Boqueron (9 September 1932). After review the zone is Boqueron plus Alto Paraguay, as in the Paraguay dossier; Presidente Hayes is outside it.

certainty.note: No treaty fixes any frontier before 1866; the Chaco, the Amazon and the Pacific desert are claims, and the Chaco block (Presidente Hayes to 1877, Boqueron and Alto Paraguay to 1935) is a claim map.

The 24th parallel with Chile (treaty of 1866, kept by the treaty of 6 August 1874) and the 1867 line with Brazil are treaty-fixed edges, but the Litoral is under Chilean occupation from 1879 and the Chaco and Acre are disputed; the era is soft overall.
Treaty lines with Chile (1904) and Brazil (1903); the Chaco Boreal frontier with Paraguay stays soft until 1935.
The Chaco front moved year by year; the July 1938 settlement fixed the line.
Treaty and demarcated lines; the final Chaco demarcation was signed on 28 April 2009.

notes:
Nine pages opened for this dossier (the budget) plus two pages opened for the Argentine dossier and cited here once each (the 1881 boundary treaty page, for the 1899 Puna lawsuit, and Gran Chaco, for the pre-1932 dispute). The Bolivia article was the identity source; the Bolivia-Peru relations and History of Bolivia pages were thin (no borders, no km2) and only back the 1839 end of the Confederation, the 6 August congress and the 1776 transfer to the Rio de la Plata.

Cliopatria's Bolivia shape (1.81 M km2, 1825-1867) is a claim map: besides the Litoral and Acre it holds 635 cells of Brazil's Amazonas, slices of Mato Grosso and Rondonia, and the whole Paraguayan Chaco (Boquerón, Alto Paraguay, Presidente Hayes). The 1867 Treaty of Ayacucho takes the Brazilian slices (pages disagree: 102,400 km2 exchange figure on the treaty page, 164,242 km2 annexed on the Acre War page, 237,233 km2 in the shape). The Chaco stays Bolivian in the shape until 1936; no page opened says who held it before the 1932 fighting, and the Gran Chaco article calls it 'a disputed territory since 1810': a gap-filler should open 'Gran Chaco' history and 'Chaco Boreal' for a pre-1932 contest.

Not settled: the year Tarija was annexed (the Confederation page says Bolivia 'occupied and annexed' it, no year; the shape holds it from 1825, so no event is recorded); the 1909 treaty with Peru (the Madre de Dios basin is not in the shape, so the 250,000 km2 is not visible); the small 1926 and 1929 western-edge changes; Bolivia's status inside the Confederation (a state of three, but Cliopatria draws one 3.2 M km2 shape); the 1866 Chile-Bolivia treaty of the 24th parallel and the 1874 treaty (not opened: the Litoral is drawn whole to 1879); the 1841 war with Peru and the Treaty of Puno of 7 June 1842 (dated by the Bolivia page, not otherwise opened).

States Cliopatria lacks: the Republic of Acre (1899-1903; slug republic-of-acre, rebel); see the report. Counterpart strings: spanish-empire (am-06), peru-bolivian-confederation, republic-of-chile, brazilian-republic (the Brazil row 'Brazilian Republic' 1890-1966 shares Q155 with three other Brazil rows), argentine-confederation (the Argentine row that runs 1834-1929).
Gazetteer names needed: Puna de Atacama (region).

After review (2026-10-19, FAIL repair): (1) Presidente Hayes is removed from the Bolivian shape from 1878 (keyframes bolivia_1877 to bolivia_1929 now adjust): 313 of the 323 cells of Paraguay's Presidente Hayes department were drawn by both this dossier and the Paraguay dossier (its /ledger/16, paraguay_1877). The pages: Presidente Hayes Department ('ultimately awarded the territory to Paraguay in 1878'), Villa Hayes (Villa Occidental founded under Carlos Antonio Lopez, 1841-1862; Argentine soldiers there in the late 1860s), Chaco War (Puerto Pacheco 1885, Bolivians evicted 1888, Pilcomayo outposts 1905, ranchers and Mennonites in the east). Disagreement: the reviewer's 'Argentine occupation 1869-1879' is not on the Villa Hayes page (it says only 'during the Paraguayan War', late 1860s) and I did not use those years. Caveat: the same evidence says Bolivia did not hold Presidente Hayes before 1878 either; keyframes 1825-1877 are left as the Bolivian claim with the facts in their notes, as asked, and the Paraguay dossier does not draw the department before 1878. The Chaco contest, the 1935 loss and the Chaco War zone are now Boqueron plus Alto Paraguay, as in the Paraguay dossier. Boqueron and Alto Paraguay are themselves a claim before 1932 (Paraguayan and Argentine ranchers and, from the 1920s, Mennonites were there): gap-filler, Chaco Boreal history 1885-1932. (2) The Puna event is redated to 1898 (confidence 2) on the Tarija Department page ('Between 1816 and 1898, the region was part of Argentina, and was ceded to Bolivia in exchange for Puna de Atacama'); the 1881 treaty page gives no year for the Bolivia-Argentina transfer and calls the land 'occupied by Chile during the Pacific war'. The reviewer's 1889 was unverified and no page opened gives it. (3) Acre: the contest is split into 1899-07 to 1900-03, 1900-11 to 1900-12 and 1902-08 to 1903-11 (Acre War page). republic-of-acre is not repaired here (its review verdict is fix) and still carries one unbroken contest 1899-1903: it must mirror these pairs. (4) Thin items: La Paz is 1898 (La Paz page, confidence 3; the Bolivia page's 'start of the twentieth century' is undated); the 1841-1842 war is a ledger pair of occupation events (Ingavi 18 November 1841; Bolivian army in southern Peru; vacated Tacna, Arica, Tarapaca in February 1842 and fell back to Moquegua and Puno; Treaty of Puno 7 June 1842 from the Bolivia page) and a war entry, and republic-of-peru has no matching event; the 1866 and 1874 treaties with Chile fix the 24th parallel, which is where the shape's Litoral already stops (23.92 S), so they are in the keyframe notes and the certainty era, not in the ledger; Tarija's annexation year is still not on any page opened (Confederation page: annexed before Argentina's declaration of 19 May 1837; Tarija page: Argentine until 1898), the pages conflict and the shape keeps Tarija from 1825.
